title: Kevin and Puzzle
observations: A liar's left neighbour is honest, so if person i is a liar the true number of liars to their left is a_(i-1) + 1: nothing about a liar's own statement is needed.
Let dp(i) count the arrangements of the first i people in which person i is honest. Person i-1 is either honest (needs a_i = a_(i-1)) or a liar with i-2 honest (needs a_i = a_(i-2) + 1).
The last person is honest or a liar, so the answer is dp(n) + dp(n-1).
nudges: If person i is lying, what do you know for certain about person i-1?
Suppose person i is honest. What are the possibilities for person i-1, and what does each force a_i to be?
Which arrangements does 'person n is honest' leave out, and how are they counted?

title: Kevin and Numbers
observations: Merging is hard to plan forwards, but backwards it is forced: a number x can only have come from floor(x/2) and ceil(x/2).
Work on b: look at its largest number. If a also contains it, cancel both. Otherwise nothing in b can ever produce it except itself, so it must be split.
Exactly n - m splits are available. Keep both multisets in priority queues; fail if a split is needed and none is left, or the largest of a exceeds the largest of b.
nudges: If x was produced by one merge, what were the two numbers?
Run the process backwards from b. What can be done with the largest number present if a does not contain it?
How many backward steps are you allowed in total?

title: Mukhammadali and the Smooth Array
observations: A changed position can be given any value, so the only constraint is on the positions you keep: their values must be non-decreasing from left to right.
Minimising the cost of what you change is the same as maximising the total cost of what you keep.

Let best(i) be the largest kept total of a non-decreasing subsequence ending at i: c_i plus the largest best(j) over j < i with a_j <= a_i. With n up to 8000 the O(n^2) table is enough; the answer is the sum of all c minus the largest best.
nudges: Suppose you have decided which positions stay untouched. When can the rest be filled in to make the array non-decreasing?
Is it easier to describe what you pay for, or what you keep?
What do you need to know about a kept subsequence in order to append one more element to it?

title: Fair and Square
observations: For three vertices in a tree, exactly one vertex c lies on all three connecting paths; every other vertex lies on none or on exactly two of them.
So in the product every value appears to an even power except a_c, which appears cubed: the triple is good exactly when a_c is a perfect square.

Count by c instead of by triple. Remove c; with component sizes s_1..s_k, triples containing c number the sum of s_i s_j, and triples not containing c the sum of s_i s_j s_l, both from one pass keeping running sums. Component sizes come from subtree sizes and n - size.
nudges: Draw three vertices in a tree and the three paths between them. How many times is each vertex of the picture used?
Given that, which single value decides whether the product is a perfect square?
Instead of going through triples, can you fix that special vertex and count the triples it is special for?

title: Minimize Fixed Points
observations: Some positions cannot move: 1, and every prime p with 2p > n, because no other number up to n shares a factor with it.
A cycle in which every number is divisible by one common prime is always good, however long it is.
Group 2..n by largest prime factor and rotate each group. A prime p with 2p <= n is grouped with 2p at least, so the only fixed points are the forced ones.
nudges: Which numbers up to n share no factor with any other number up to n?
If several positions are all multiples of the same prime, in how many ways may you shuffle the values among them?
How can you split 2..n into groups, each sharing a prime, so that as few groups as possible have size one?

title: Elections in Saransk (easy version)
observations: The lcm equals the product exactly when the chosen numbers are pairwise coprime, i.e. every prime divides at most one of them.
Primes do not interact. For one prime, either nobody uses it, or exactly one voter i does, with any exponent from 1 up to its exponent in a_i: that is 1 + (sum of its exponents over all a_i) ways.
Multiply that over every prime that divides some a_i, factorising with a smallest-prime-factor sieve.
nudges: When is the least common multiple of several numbers equal to their product?
Fix one prime. In how many ways can it be handed out among the voters?
Do the choices made for two different primes restrict each other?

title: A Bit Odd
observations: A position with no legal move is a string of equal characters, so try to win in one move: delete all the 1s (plus some 0s) or all the 0s (plus some 1s). That works exactly when some 0 has an odd number of 1s before it, or some 1 has an odd number of 0s after it.
If neither holds, the string is an optional 0, then blocks each equal to 00 or 11, then an optional 1.

In such a string, split any block between the removed part and the rest and both parts get the same character; blocks kept together add an even amount. So the removed part and the remainder have the same inversion parity: after any legal move the remainder is itself a legal move, and the opponent deletes all of it.
So the first player wins exactly when the string is not of that block form.
nudges: What do the positions with no legal move look like, and when can you reach one in a single move?
If no single move wins, what must the string look like, read two characters at a time?
In that case, compare the parity of inversions in the part you delete with the parity in the part you leave. What does that hand your opponent?

title: Array Replacement
observations: Look at the differences d_i = a_(i+1) - a_i. The operation at i swaps d_(i-1) and d_i and changes nothing else.
It is allowed when a_(i-1) and a_(i+1) have the same parity, i.e. when d_(i-1) + d_i is even: the two differences have the same parity.

So a difference can never pass one of the other parity: each maximal run of same-parity differences can be sorted freely, and nothing else is reachable. Sort every run in increasing order and rebuild from a_1.
nudges: What does the operation do to the two gaps on either side of a_i?
What does the parity condition say about those two gaps?
If neighbouring gaps can be swapped only when they have the same parity, which rearrangements of the gaps are possible?

title: Inversion Value of a Permutation
observations: Count the opposite: segments with no inversion. A segment has no inversion exactly when it is increasing, so cut the permutation at every descent into increasing blocks.
If every pair of elements from different blocks is inverted, the inversion-free segments are exactly those inside one block: a block of length L gives L(L-1)/2 of them.

So you need block lengths summing to n with the L(L-1)/2 summing to n(n-1)/2 - k: a small table over (elements used, segments so far). Then fill the first block with the largest numbers in increasing order, the next block with the next largest, and so on.
nudges: Which is easier to describe: a segment that contains an inversion, or one that contains none?
If the permutation is made of increasing runs, how many inversion-free segments does a run of length L contribute?
Given the run lengths, how do you place the numbers so that no segment crossing two runs is increasing?

title: Binary Bubble Sort Inversions
observations: Trying small arrays shows a bubble only moves one element in effect: the first 1 ends up at the very end. A reverse bubble moves the last 0 to the very front.
Moving the first 1 to the end removes one inversion for every 0 after it: (number of 0s) minus (number of leading 0s). The reverse case removes (number of 1s) minus (number of trailing 1s).

Leading 0s and trailing 1s never matter again, so keep two pointers around the active middle part: a bubble drops its first element, a reverse bubble its last, then skip new leading 0s and trailing 1s while updating the counts.
nudges: Run one bubble by hand on 1 1 0 1 0 0. Compare before and after: which elements have effectively moved?
When that one element moves to the end, which inversions disappear?
Which parts of the array can no longer take part in any inversion, and can you stop looking at them?

title: Tea Blend
observations: The number of divisors is the product of (exponent + 1), which is odd exactly when every exponent is even: the number is a perfect square.

Only the parity of each exponent matters, and multiplying numbers XORs their sets of odd-exponent primes. So F(i, j) is a square exactly when a_i and the product of the first j elements have the same set.

Keep a map from the set (hashed) of each prefix to how often it occurs, and add up, over i, the count for the set of a_i. Sets with more than 7 primes can be ignored: no single a_i up to 10^6 has that many.
nudges: Which numbers have an odd number of divisors?
For a product to be a perfect square, what must be true of each prime's exponent in the two factors?
What short summary of a prefix product is enough to tell whether one more factor makes it a square?

title: Omg Graph
observations: Pick any edge j on the path and use (its weight + the largest weight) as the cost. That is never less than the true cost and equals it when j is the smallest edge, so minimising over all choices of j gives the answer.
For a fixed edge (u, v, w) you may walk 1 to u, cross it, then v to n (paths need not be simple), so you need the smallest possible largest-edge from 1 to every vertex and from n to every vertex.
Smallest largest-edge is found by the settle-the-nearest method with max in place of +; the same proof works. Then take the minimum over edges of w + max(to u, w, from v), trying both directions.
nudges: Suppose you were told which edge is the smallest on the best path. What would be left to minimise?
What happens to the cost if you pretend some other edge of the path is the smallest?
How do you find, for every vertex, the path from 1 whose largest edge is as small as possible?

title: Chicken Jockey
observations: A mob that takes fall damage lands at the bottom of a stack, so no mob takes fall damage twice.

If a mob takes more than 1 fall damage, the mob directly below it was killed by attacks alone (otherwise that mob was itself at the bottom, and the fall would be 1). So it is best done in the original stack, where the fall is as large as possible: i - 1.

So for each mob there are two cases. Let best(i) be the fewest attacks for the first i mobs: either mob i falls 1 when the mob below dies, best(i-1) + h_i - 1, or mob i-1 is killed by hand and mob i falls i - 1, best(i-2) + h_(i-1) + max(0, h_i - (i-1)).
nudges: After a mob has taken fall damage, where is it in its stack, and can it fall again?
If a mob takes more than one point of fall damage, how did the mob just below it die?
What are the only ways mob i can be dealt with, given what happens to mob i-1?

title: Nastiness of Segments
observations: Fix l. As d grows, d itself strictly increases while min(a_l..a_(l+d)) never increases, so they can be equal for at most one d: the answer to a query is 0 or 1.
If there is such a d, it is the smallest d with d >= min(a_l..a_(l+d)), because 'd minus the minimum' only ever grows. Find that d by halving and check for equality.
Each test needs a range minimum under point updates: a segment tree. Halving over it costs log^2 per query; walking down the tree once brings it to log.
nudges: For a fixed left end, how do d and the minimum of the first d + 1 elements each change as d grows?
How many times can a strictly increasing sequence meet a non-increasing one?
Which d would you test first, and what does the result of the test tell you about where the meeting point is?

title: Flip the Bit (Hard Version)
observations: Mark each cell as right or wrong and pad both ends with right. A flip of [l, r] changes only the two boundaries at l-1 and r, so the task is to remove every boundary between a right and a wrong cell.
The range must contain a special index, so the two boundaries it touches lie in different regions between special indices.
With S boundaries in total and X in the fullest region: each operation removes at most two, and at most one from any region, so at least max(S/2, X) operations are needed.

That many are enough: pair boundaries from different regions while no region holds more than half; leftovers from a dominant region are removed one per operation against a throwaway position on the other side.
nudges: Instead of the cells, look at the places where a right cell meets a wrong one. What does one flip do to those places?
What does the rule about special indices say about the two places one flip can touch?
What two different reasons stop you from using fewer operations, and can a pairing scheme meet both?

title: Dr. Agos's Dark Mode
observations: 2 is -1 mod 3, so the powers of 2 alternate +1, -1. With the alternating prefix sum p_i = sum of (-1)^j s_j mod 3, the segment (l, r) is divisible by 3 exactly when p_(l-1) = p_r.
So f(s) is the number of equal pairs among the n+1 prefix values: C(c0,2) + C(c1,2) + C(c2,2), smallest when the three counts differ by at most one.

A 0 repeats the current prefix value and a 1 changes it, so three 1s make four constant blocks. Put the 1s near n/3, 2n/3 and the end; trying the two nearest positions for each (eight candidates) always contains a balanced one.
nudges: What are the powers of 2 modulo 3?
Can you define a running quantity such that a segment is divisible by 3 exactly when it takes the same value at both ends?
If the running quantity takes each of its three values c0, c1, c2 times, how many bad segments are there, and which split of n+1 makes that smallest?

title: Wonderful Lightbulbs
observations: Every operation flips four bulbs, so the number of lit bulbs stays odd; that alone does not locate anything.
Two of the four bulbs are on the line x = u and two on x = u + 1, so the parity of lit bulbs on every vertical line never changes: exactly one vertical line has an odd count, the treasure's.
The same holds for the diagonals x + y = c (two bulbs on u + v, two on u + v + 1). The odd vertical line and the odd diagonal meet at the treasure.
nudges: How many bulbs does one operation flip, and what does that keep fixed?
Split the four flipped bulbs by their x coordinate. What stays fixed on each vertical line?
One family of lines gives one coordinate. Is there another family of lines that each operation also hits an even number of times?

title: Rigged Bracket Sequence
observations: Replace ( by +1 and ) by -1 and watch the prefix sums. A prefix that contains none or all of the chosen positions keeps its sum. A prefix that contains only some of them loses its last chosen character and gains the last character of the whole subsequence.
So if the subsequence ends with (, nothing can go wrong: every such subsequence is fine, 2^(k-1) of them ending at position k.
If it ends with ), a prefix sum drops by 2 wherever a chosen ( was the last chosen character so far, so the prefix sums from that ( up to the next chosen position must all be at least 2.

Count those with a table: D(i) = number of ways to choose the part up to i with i chosen; D(j) feeds D(i) if S_j is ) or the prefix sums between j and i stay at least 2. Running totals of D with two pointers make it linear.
nudges: Turn the brackets into +1 and -1. For one prefix, which characters enter and which leave when the chosen positions are shifted?
What happens if the last chosen character is an opening bracket?
If the last chosen character is a closing bracket, between which chosen positions can a prefix sum fall, and by how much?

title: Clean Substrings
observations: Let b_i = 1 where s_i and s_(i+1) differ. Inverting a clean substring changes only the b just before it and the b at its end, so one coin clears at most two 1s: the beauty is ceil(sum of b / 2).

The sum of b over a substring is odd exactly when its first and last characters differ, and there are cnt0 x cnt1 such substrings. So the total of the ceilings is (total of the sums + cnt0 x cnt1) / 2.
The total of the sums is found per position: a 1 at b_i lies in i (n - i) substrings. A modification changes only two entries of b and the two counts, so each update is O(1).
nudges: Mark every place where two neighbouring characters differ. What does one operation do to those marks?
For which substrings is the number of marks odd? Can you count them without looking at the marks?
In how many substrings does one particular mark appear?

title: She knows...
observations: Flipping the colour of one cell changes the number of differing neighbour pairs by an amount with the parity of its number of neighbours. So cells with an even number of neighbours never affect the parity.
The cells with an odd number of neighbours are the border cells that are not corners. The parity of the count equals the parity of the number of black cells among them.
If all of those cells are already painted, the answer is 2^(free cells) or 0. If at least one is free, exactly half of all colourings work: 2^(free cells - 1).
nudges: Recolour a single cell. By how much can the number of differing neighbour pairs change, and what decides whether that change is odd?
Which cells of the board have an odd number of neighbours?
If one of those cells is still unpainted, how do the colourings with an even count compare in number with those with an odd count?

title: Rada and the Chamomile Valley
observations: A lane that every walk from 1 to n must use disconnects 1 from n when removed, so it is a bridge; and it lies on any one path from 1 to n you care to pick.

Conversely a bridge that lies on one chosen path from 1 to n is used by every walk: removing it splits the graph with 1 and n on different sides. So the forced lanes are exactly (bridges) intersected with (one path from 1 to n).
For the queries, start one breadth-first search from all endpoints of forced lanes at distance 0; each house then knows its nearest forced lane (carry the smallest lane index along for ties).
nudges: If the walkers can avoid a lane, what does removing that lane do to the connection between house 1 and house n?
Take one particular path from 1 to n. Which of its lanes could the walkers have avoided by going another way?
How can every house learn its distance to the nearest of many special houses in a single pass?

title: Fallen Leaves
observations: Look at one edge. If the number of leaves below it is even they can all be paired below it; if odd, exactly one pair must cross it. So with an even number of leaves the answer is the number of edges with an odd count of leaves below.
With an odd number of leaves one leaf is left out. Leaving out leaf x flips the parity of every edge on the path from the root to x: odd edges are saved, even edges are added.
So choose the leaf that maximises (odd edges minus even edges) on its root path, computed by one pass up the tree, and subtract that from the count.
nudges: Fix one edge. How many of the chosen pairs are forced to cross it, in terms of the number of leaves on one side?
If one leaf is going to be left unpaired, which edges change their answer to the previous question?
How do you find, for the whole tree at once, the leaf whose removal helps the most?

title: Generational Triplets
observations: The conditions say 2b = a + c and b = a xor c, so 2 (a xor c) = a + c.
Since a + c = (a xor c) + 2 (a and c), this becomes a xor c = 2 (a and c): the XOR pattern is the AND pattern shifted up by one bit. b is then determined, and a < b < c follows from a < c.
Count pairs a < c <= n bit by bit from the top, remembering: whether c is already below n, whether a is already below c, and the AND bit that the previous XOR bit demands here.
nudges: Use the two conditions to eliminate b. What single equation do a and c satisfy?
How is a + c related to a xor c and a and c?
Reading the bits of a and c from the top, what must you carry from one bit position to the next to check that equation and the bound c <= n?

title: N-MEX (Constructive Version)
observations: With i numbers written, the (n-i+1)-th missing number is at least n - i and at most n, so n - i <= a_i <= n is forced.
Appending one number can fill at most one gap while the index of the gap asked for drops by one, so a_i >= a_(i+1) is forced too.

Those two conditions are enough. Let S be the numbers in 0..n that never appear in a. When a_i < a_(i-1) write a huge number (it fills no gap); when a_i = a_(i-1) write the largest unused element of S.
nudges: After i numbers are written, what are the smallest and largest possible values of the gap you are asked about?
How can the answer change when one more number is written and you ask for the gap one place earlier?
If you only ever write numbers that never appear among the a_i, or numbers too large to matter, which of the two should you write at each step?

title: A Prime Flood (Easy Version)
observations: An operation never changes the order of two values, so once the smallest and largest of a subsequence are equal, everything between is equal: f(b) depends only on min(b) and max(b).

Let g(x, y) be the best common value for the pair x <= y, with g(x, x) = x. If some prime divides y but not x, lower y alone: g(x, y) = g(x, y-1). Otherwise every prime of y also divides x and both drop: g(x, y) = g(x-1, y-1).
Values are at most 3000, so fill the whole table (the second case is x divisible by the product of the distinct primes of y).
Then count subsequences by their minimum and maximum: with c_v copies of v, the pair x < y has (2^(c_x) - 1)(2^(c_y) - 1) 2^(copies strictly between) subsequences.
nudges: Can an operation ever make a smaller value overtake a larger one?
For just two values x < y, which primes let you lower y without touching x, and what if there are none?
Once you know the answer for every pair (smallest, largest), how many subsequences have a given smallest and largest value?

title: Sliding Tree
observations: Watch the longest path (the diameter). One sliding operation changes the length of any path by at most 1, so the diameter grows by at most 1 per operation.
A path graph has diameter n - 1, so with diameter l at the start at least (n - 1) - l operations are needed.

That bound is reached: take a longest path, find a vertex u on it that has a neighbour v off it, and slide with b = u, c = v and a = the neighbour of u on the path towards one end. The longest path gets one longer every time.
So the answer is any such operation; if no vertex of a longest path has an off-path neighbour, the tree is already a path.
nudges: What single number measures how far the tree is from being a path, and what is it for a path?
By how much can one operation change the length of a given path?
If you want that number to grow by exactly one, where in the tree should the operation be applied?

title: Twin Polynomials
observations: Rewrite the condition: for every i, a_i equals the sum of all j with a_j = i.

Looking at the smallest positive index that misbehaves gives a contradiction, so for every i > 0 there are only three cases: a_i = 0, a_i = i, or a_i = j and a_j = i for some other j. The polynomial is a pairing of some indices, with every unpaired index choosing 0 or itself.
With nothing fixed, the count for indices 1..i satisfies D(i) = 2 D(i-1) + (i-1) D(i-2): index i is alone (two choices) or paired with one of the i - 1 others.
Fixed coefficients either contradict the three cases (answer 0) or simply remove decided indices, after which the same recurrence counts the free ones.
nudges: Write the condition f = g coefficient by coefficient. What must a_i be, in terms of the other coefficients?
Suppose some index does not fit a simple pattern. What can you say about the smallest such index?
Once you know each index is alone or paired with exactly one other, how do you count the arrangements of i indices from smaller counts?

title: Wonderful Teddy Bears
observations: Write black as 0 and pink as 1. Sorting three neighbours is one of four moves: 010 to 001 and 101 to 011 remove one inversion; 100 to 001 and 110 to 011 remove two.
So with x inversions at least x/2 instructions are needed, and ideally only the two-inversion moves are used. Using only those, you get stuck at 0...0 1010...10 1...1.

The two-inversion moves shift a 0 by two places, so they never change b, the number of 0s on even positions; the one-inversion moves change b by exactly 1. In the sorted row b must be floor(a/2), where a is the number of 0s.
So at least d = |floor(a/2) - b| one-inversion moves are needed, the remaining x - d inversions go two at a time, and (x + d) / 2 is achievable.
nudges: List the different things one instruction can do to three neighbours. How many inversions does each remove?
Suppose you only ever used the instructions that remove two inversions. What pattern can they not fix?
The best instructions move a 0 two places. What property of the positions of the 0s do they leave unchanged, and what must that property be at the end?
